newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait backs U.S. deployment, seeks Arab support.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait backs U.S. deployment, seeks Arab support.

text.p: Kuwait lobbied Arab allies to support a display of U.S. military muscle in the Gulf but many appeared sceptical about the need to mete out further punishment to Gulf War foe Iraq.
Kuwaitis, still seething about Iraq's 1990-91 occupation, applauded a U.S. decision to send 3,500 more U.S. troops to Kuwait to deter further trouble from President Saddam Hussein.
The wealthy Gulf oil state sent envoys to Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Syria and Bahrain to rally support for its decision to allow U.S. troops and warplanes to deploy on its territory.

President Bill Clinton said on Tuesday he had ordered the U.S. ground troops to Kuwait from Fort Hood, Texas "to keep Saddam Hussein in a box", following the deployment in Kuwait of eight Stealth bombers and over 20 other U.S. warplanes last week.
"When the Americans are here, I am safe," said a Kuwaiti businessman who gave his name only as Salah.
"The deployment is a popular desire of every Kuwaiti," political writer Fouad al-Hashem told Reuters.
"We will close our ears to all Arab calls not to deploy the troops. It seems the only way to make them feel the way we do is for Saddam Hussein to occupy the whole Arab world.
But some diplomats in Kuwait said that with tension between Washington and Iraq apparently dropping in recent days, it was hard to understand the need to demonstrate more U.S. muscle.
"Even after the tension drops, the Americans keep sending more troops. I don't see the need for them at all. Can you move in all this force without using it?" one diplomat said.

Kuwait's envoys, Defence Minister Sheikh Ahmad Hamoud al-Jaber al-Sabah and Information Minister Sheikh Saud Nasser al-Saud al-Sabah, told their Arab hosts that Iraq last week called the deployment of the Stealth an act of war.
Kuwait says this is a new threat that has not been retracted by a country that occupied it for seven months.

While Egypt and Syria continue to support Kuwait's right to defend itself if attacked by Iraq, they have not endorsed the latest U.S. flap with Iraq and oppose America's September 3 and 4 cruise missile attacks against targets in southern Iraq.

The confrontation between Iraq and the United States began late last month when Baghdad's forces intervened to help a Kurdish faction in northern Iraq -- an area closed to them since the end of the Gulf war in 1991.
Cairo and Damascus, like most of the Arab world, saw as legitimate Baghdad's action in northern Iraq which did not violate U.N. Gulf crisis resolutions or international norms.
Only Kuwait among Arab states gave public support for the U.S. strikes.
Some of America's other Gulf Arab allies say privately they are irritated by what they see as a go-it-alone U.S. policy over Iraq that has ignored their security and political concerns.
Saudi silence over the U.S. actions against fellow Arab Iraq was widely seen as disapproval of American insensitivity towards the political impact of such strikes on Gulf Arab opinion.
Iraq said the U.S. troop deployment planned for the next few days showed Washington was planning another attack.
Some diplomats in Kuwait said the deployment of the U.S. First Cavalry Division troops could be seen by some Arab states as prolonging rather than resolving the latest flare-up.
"This could be seen as a new escalation that would give the Iraqis the moral right to contest the legality of the no-fly zones," a senior diplomat said.
